items.title: Quad9 to exit France
items.content:
Starting November 24, Quad9 will no longer be able to offer its free cyberprotection service to users located in France.

The French courts yesterday handed down an unfavorable ruling against Quad9 in a major case that undermines the transparency and stability of the internet. This decision in favor of beIN forces Quad9 to block the recursive DNS resolution for a number of domain names for users located in France.

The good news is the court significantly reduced the financial penalty, from €580,000 to €1,000 per day. However, for Quad9, this has never been just a financial issue: it is a matter of principle.

We cannot comply with this ruling over the long term while remaining faithful to our mission to protect your privacy, defend you against cyber threats, and preserve the integrity of the internet. For us, recursive DNS resolution is a neutral and passive service. We categorically refuse to alter or lie to you about the DNS responses you receive in a way that opposes your expectations.

This ruling forces an untenable position upon us. Compliance is technically unfeasible, and implementation directly contradicts our mandate to serve the public. As a result, we have made the difficult decision to withdraw Quad9 services from France as of Tuesday, November 24. We deeply regret that French internet users will be left without an alternative that can adequately protect their cybersecurity while remaining compliant with European privacy law.

beIN, a Qatari company with offices in France, previously sought to force Quad9 to block resolution for a set of domain names they assert are participating in copyright infringement of its audiovisual rights on sports event broadcasts. Quad9 has no association with these domain names, nor with the operators of the websites. The French courts have fundamentally misunderstood the working of the internet and the role of the domain name system and have allowed a financial penalty to apply to Quad9 if we do not block DNS responses to users in France.

Quad9 is a Swiss public-benefit, nonprofit foundation established for the explicit purpose of protecting the cybersecurity of internet users. We charge nothing for our service and serve all people and organizations which seek to improve the security and privacy of their internet use. Our core values are to make privacy, security, and integrity available to all internet users, and our mission is to universally apply these guiding principles to recursive DNS resolution services in order to serve end users.

We want to be very clear: we do not condone content piracy. Quad9 exists to create a safer, more trustworthy internet experience for end users. We offer global blocking as an option for malicious cyberactivity against users worldwide. We do not block content, and we give users the choice to use our threat blocking services, or not, based on their interests and needs. Content piracy needs to be dealt with at the source: the place where the infringing content is published. Forcing uninvolved third parties to break the fundamental operating principles of the internet to benefit individual parties to the detriment of the global internet-using public is misguided, counter-productive, and distracts from actual solutions addressing the hosting of the content directly, or the market pressures which cause piracy to exist in the first place. Not only are DNS recursive resolvers, like Quad9, the wrong actors to address piracy, but applying legal pressure to Quad9 will also have vast unintended consequences harming the cybersecurity of hundreds of millions of innocent internet users.

For Quad9, complying with this ruling is impossible. We have no database of users associating them with jurisdictions. Our service is free to the public and does not require sign-up or proof of identity. Recursive DNS is so fundamental to the underlying operation of the internet that there is no method to map users’ jurisdictions reliably, nor do we think there should be a way…

items.title: Docker is weird
items.content:
I decided to make my own container runtime for fun, and even though I’m still early on, I’ve learned that Docker is weird . Here’s some weird things I learned about Docker.

Unlike VMs, containers are just processes with special restrictions on them. Your kernel is still running that process! And if you know where to look, you can even find that process in /proc.

There’s not really a linux feature that’s just “containers” either. Instead, containers are really 5 different linux kernel features in trenchcoat.

Namespaces hide what the host and container can see, cgroups limit container resource usage, and there’s a whole bunch of networking magic I don’t understand that lets you isolate a container’s network.

Images are just folders that Docker puts somewhere and then calls chroot (or pivot_root ) to make that folder your container process’s new root directory. So if you run docker run -it --rm ubuntu /bin/bash , Docker is going to:

Docker’s container runtime, runc , is written in Go, and Go has some design choices that make it less suited for a container runtime. Go’s runtime is natively multi-threaded. That’s a really cool feature, but it leads to some challenges in runc .

Many of the Linux syscalls a container runtime needs to make have to be done in a single-threaded environment, so runc has a crazy C module that runs before Go’s runtime initializes so it can run those syscalls.

Go also doesn’t have fork! Fork only forks the main thread, so it’s kind of a footgun in a runtime like Go’s. But a container runtime really wants to fork, set up a bunch of restrictions, and then exec the process you actually put in docker run . To get around this, runc execs /proc/self/exe with a special command line arguement that identifies it as a child process to approximate a fork.

This is pretty easy to miss if you, like me, run Docker in MacOS. Many of the Linux kernel APIs that container runtimes use require, or at least used to, to be run as root, so the Docker daemon usually runs as root. I can only imagine that container security is a very tough job.

This seems better these days. The big exception seems to be networking. If you’re running a rootless container runtime, it looks like it has to reimplement the whole networking stack in userspace to actually give you the same features!

I’ve only just started my own container runtime, and I already feel like I’ve learned so much about Docker. Writing your own version of a tool you use is a great way to learn about it!
items.title_ko: Docker는 생각보다 이상하다: 직접 만든 컨테이너 런타임에서 배운 것들
items.summary_ko: 작성자는 재미 삼아 직접 컨테이너 런타임을 만들며 Docker의 동작 방식을 알게 되었다고 밝혔습니다. 컨테이너는 가상 머신이 아니라 특수한 제약이 걸린 프로세스이며, 여러 리눅스 커널 기능이 함께 동작하여 만들어집니다. 이미지는 루트 디렉터리를 바꾸는 폴더이고, 런타임 runc는 Go로 작성되어 있는데 Go의 다중 스레드 특성 때문에 어려움이 있다고 설명합니다.
items.content_ko: 작성자는 컨테이너 런타임을 직접 만들어 보면서 Docker가 이상하다는 것을 알게 되었다고 밝혔습니다. 컨테이너는 VM과 달리 특정 제약이 걸린 프로세스일 뿐이며, 호스트 커널이 그 프로세스를 그대로 실행하고 있어 /proc에서 찾을 수 있습니다. '컨테이너'라는 단일 리눅스 기능은 없으며, 실제로는 다섯 가지 리눅스 커널 기능이 합쳐진 것입니다. 네임스페이스는 호스트와 컨테이너가 서로 보는 범위를 숨기고, cgroups는 자원 사용량을 제한하며, 네트워크 관련 기능으로 컨테이너의 네트워크를 격리합니다. 이미지는 Docker가 어딘가에 두는 폴더일 뿐이고, chroot나 pivot_root를 호출해 그 폴더를 컨테이너 프로세스의 새 루트 디렉터리로 만듭니다. Docker의 런타임 runc는 Go로 작성되어 있는데, Go의 네이티브 다중 스레드 구조가 컨테이너 런타임에는 어려움을 낳는다고 설명합니다. 원문은 중간에서 끊겨 있습니다.

items.title: Getty Images files for bankruptcy amid mounting debt and AI competition
items.content:
Getty Images on Wednesday filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protections as part of a restructuring plan to take the flailing stock photo provider private.

It listed assets of $1 billion to $10 billion, and liabilities in the same range.

The content provider announced last week that it was planning to file in Delaware bankruptcy court after its near $4 billion merger with rival Shutterstock collapsed due to British antitrust challenges.

Getty Images on Wednesday filed for bankruptcy. Timon – stock.adobe.com

Getty Images – which has supplied photos and video for news agencies for more than 30 years – has been struggling amid a pile of debt and mounting competition from AI image generators.

The company will receive up to $533 million in fresh equity from affiliates of the Getty family – descendants of oil tycoon J. Paul Getty – and Koch Equity Development. Those parties will own 100% of the company once it is taken private.

It said Wednesday that it has launched a solicitation process to secure formal approval for its restructuring plan, and that it expects the reorganization to be completed by the end of the year.

Getty Images will continue normal operations in the meantime, with no impact on contributors, partners, customers, employees or vendors, the company said.

Financing from Koch Equity Development of roughly $143 million will support the restructuring process.

The photo archive entered into a 30-day grace period after failing to make interest payments due Sept. 1 on unsecured notes.

It said it had the cash necessary to make the payments, but opted to pursue a restructuring.
items.title_ko: Getty Images, 누적 부채와 AI 경쟁 속에 파산 보호 신청

items.content_ko: Getty Images는 수요일 구조조정 계획의 일환으로 Chapter 11 파산 보호를 신청했으며, 이를 통해 회사를 비공개 기업으로 전환할 계획입니다. 자산과 부채는 각각 10억 달러에서 100억 달러 사이로 제시되었습니다. 회사는 지난주 Delaware 파산법원에 신청할 계획을 밝혔는데, 이는 약 40억 달러 규모의 Shutterstock 합병이 영국 반독점 문제로 무산된 뒤의 조치입니다. Getty Images는 30년 넘게 뉴스 기관에 사진과 영상을 공급해 왔으나, 부채 증가와 AI 이미지 생성기와의 경쟁 심화로 어려움을 겪어 왔습니다. Getty 가문의 계열사와 Koch Equity Development는 최대 5억 3,300만 달러의 신규 자본을 투입하며, 비공개 전환 후 회사의 지분 100%를 소유하게 됩니다. 회사는 구조조정 계획에 대한 공식 승인을 받기 위한 절차를 시작했으며, 연말까지 재편을 마칠 것으로 예상하고 있습니다. 그동안 회사는 정상 영업을 계속한다고 밝혔습니다.

items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

식별 코드 기준으로 당일 글 10개, 댓글 20개 작성 시 대왕디시콘을 3일간 사용할 수 있습니다.

즐겨찾기 폴더 추가는 즐겨찾기 on 후 우측의 폴더 아이콘을 터치하여 추가할 수 있습니다.

items.title: eMudhra to exit global SSL/TLS certificate business
items.content:
Will Sharpen Focus on Core Enterprise Solutions and trust services other than SSL/TLS

BENGALURU, INDIA, October 22, 2026 - eMudhra Limited (BSE: 543533 | NSE: EMUDHRA), a global digital trust company, today announced that its Board has decided to voluntarily withdraw from the global SSL/TLS certificate business.

Mr. V. Srinivasan, Chairman, eMudhra Limited referred to the recent incident relating to its global SSL/TLS certificate and indicated that eMudhra handled the recent incident diligently, revoking the affected CAs within 14 hours of discovery and disclosing promptly. There were no end entity certificates issued out of the affected CA’s. Its infrastructure was not compromised and no data was breached. All physical and logical security controls remained intact.

He added that global SSL/TLS is a small part of eMudhra’s business contributing to about 1% of the global revenue. Due to increasing data sovereignty & compliance requirements, complexity and cost associated with this business is increasing over the years. This, paired with the fact that some of the large entities issue the SSL/TLS free of cost, the business potential and RoI of this line of business also has considerably reduced for eMudhra when measured against our cumulative revenue base.

However, the level of social media amplification around this incident has brought scrutiny that is out of proportion to SSL/TLS’s place in our business. In view of this, after detailed deliberations our board has concluded that withdrawing from global SSL/TLS is the right decision for eMudhra and its shareholders. For many certifying authorities, SSL/TLS is the whole business. For eMudhra it is one part of a much broader digital solutions portfolio. We will put our energy where we create the most value for customers with Sharpened Focus on Core Enterprise Solutions and trust services other than SSL/TLS.

Our G1 RSA roots will continue to serve customers until this transition is complete as we work with browser programs and our customers to enable this transition. eMudhra will reach out to affected customers to replace any certificate free of cost from partners through the transition. Revocation and certificate status services will keep running until every issued certificate has expired or been replaced. eMudhra will complete its remaining commitments to the browser root programs, including a full root-cause report.

eMudhra’s global SSL/TLS infrastructure runs separately from its other operations. The company’s Global digital signature certificate (DSC), eSign, and other signing services, including those in India, its enterprise PKI Solutions (emCA, CertiNext platforms), emSigner eSignature Suite, and its identity and authentication solutions (SecurePass, emAS) are not affected and continue to operate as normal.

With over 17 years of expertise, eMudhra is a global provider of digital identity, trust, and security solutions, enabling secure digital transformation for banks and financial institutions (BFSI), enterprises, and governments across more than 35 countries worldwide. Its product suite spans CertiNext (PKI and certificate lifecycle management), SecurePass (identity and access management, multi-factor authentication and converged identity), and PrivaTrust (data discovery and consent management for global data-privacy compliance and DSARs), delivering high-assurance digital trust at population scale.

items.title: UUIDv7 doesn't have the properties you think it does
items.content:
Most blog posts about UUIDv7 tout these benefits:

But none of these properties are strictly held.

Certain RFC compliant implementations of UUIDv7 violate these properties to extreme degrees.

The only useful property UUIDv7 appears to strictly provide is uniqueness and therefore collision resistance.

so this post explores the other properties.

Superficially, it seems that embedding a timestamp in the ID can remove the need to track the creation time in a separate database column, providing marginally more efficient database operations.

If you need to list things ordered by creation time very often, it’s useful if the primary index gives that behavior, removing the need for another index.

Unfortunately, the timestamp embedded in a UUIDv7 ID may not relate to the object creation time.

The Postgres docs for uuid_extract_timestamp

helpfully warn that “the extracted timestamp is not necessarily exactly equal to the time the UUID was generated”.

allows implementations to alter the timestamp field, using values that aren’t strictly derived from the system clock.

This relates to the tension between UUID monotonicity and timestamp accuracy.

In certain scenarios, the difference between the timestamp and the current time can be arbitrarily large.

Implementations MAY alter the actual timestamp. — RFC 9562 §6.1

This specification makes no requirement or guarantee about how close the clock value needs to be to the actual time. — RFC 9562 §6.1

… implementations MAY increment the timestamp ahead of the actual time … — RFC 9562 §6.2

Incrementing the timestamp ahead of the system clock is an interesting problem.

If the generator is seeing so much load that a counter field is regularly overflowing then the timestamp could accelerate into the future.

Using a sufficiently large counter would be wise and the RFC says the minimum size SHOULD be 12 bits.

A counter overflow would require a pretty aggressive creation rate, over 4,096 IDs per millisecond per node, which is beyond the limits of many systems.

This overflow becomes relevant, however, if the timestamp freezes; which I’ll discuss in a later section.

One prominent implementation that increments the timestamp is the Python standard library’s UUIDv7.

The increment happens only in certain circumstances, like when the counter overflows.

Unfortunately, the generator can get stuck in an increment cycle if the clock ever jumps backwards and the timestamp can race ahead of the system time by an arbitrarily large amount.

We expect the difference to be 3600 seconds (one hour) as the implementation refuses to allow the embedded timestamp to jump backwards and we expect the difference to decrease as the system clock catches up to the frozen timestamp.

But when the load is above one ID per millisecond the difference will increase without bound.

At lower loads it will take longer for the system clock to catch the timestamp, but we don’t see the runaway effect.

shows Python developers reasoning that this is consistent with the RFC, is consistent with other implementations, and that there isn’t “much we can do” on a “flawed system”.

I think these points are correct as I see this same behavior in other implementations.

Nevertheless, it would be helpful if existing UUIDv7 implementations could handle system clock jumps without runaway behavior.

There are many real-world examples of clocks jumping backwards,

even decades out of sync in time-sensitive environments.

Embedding the timestamp in the ID means that you cannot share the ID without also sharing the timestamp.

It’s pretty difficult to think of an example where this really matters.

One example could be a user profile page that doesn’t disclose when the account was created, but the UUIDv7 ID in the URL leaks the high-precision timestamp.

This issue would typically be very low on my list of security concerns because I find much more severe problems when I do security assessments.

ID에 타임스탬프를 넣으면 생성 시각을 별도 데이터베이스 컬럼으로 관리할 필요가 줄어드는 것처럼 보이지만, 포함된 타임스탬프가 객체 생성 시각과 같지 않을 수 있습니다. items.title: Incident Report: unsanctioned agent behaviour during cyber testing | AISI Work
items.content:
You can access the full technical report here.

AISI’s role is to evaluate and understand the capabilities of frontier AI models, surfacing potential risks before they reach the public. To assess what these models can do, including whether they could be misused for cyberattacks, we test them under deliberately permissive conditions: with access to the open internet, and with some safety filters disabled.

On 28 th July 2026, AISI's Security Team detected unusual data transfers leaving our research systems during a routine cyber evaluation. On investigation, we found that some of the agents being tested had engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations. We declared a security incident and, within roughly one hour of discovery, had contained it and begun a full investigation.

The incident stemmed from a single evaluation where agents were given a task of solving a cyber security challenge. We ran this challenge 122 times across several models. Our investigation found that in 10 of those runs, an AI agent took autonomous, unsanctioned action on the live internet, targeting real people and organisations. In total, we catalogued 19 such actions. Almost all of this behaviour (17 actions) came from a single model, Anthropic's Mythos 5, with 2 actions involving OpenAI's GPT-5.6-Sol with cyber classifiers (mechanisms to prevent misuse) disabled. In the most serious case, an agent tried to insert malicious code into an open-source project. In an attempt to get the code approved, the agent engaged in social engineering  — creating fake online identities and using them to pressure the project's maintainer to approve the code. A human maintainer caught and refused to approve the malicious code.

These attempts were unsuccessful, and our investigations have not evidenced any resulting real-world harm. But this is the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real-world.

Importantly, this was not a case of a model escaping its secure test environment, or ‘sandbox’. As was standard in our cyber testing, we had intentionally permitted internet access, and model-provider cyber classifiers were deliberately disabled - conditions that do not reflect how frontier models are made available to the public. We do this to best assess the maximum capability of models. These configuration choices have been common practice in frontier AI evaluations. The specific models in question, in the configurations in which we tested them are not commercially available and there is no clear indication of similar activity outside of testing scenarios.

Ahead of publishing this blog, we notified GitHub (the developer platform accessed during the evaluation) of the agents' malicious activity, which included actions that GitHub has confirmed violated their terms of service. We worked together with GitHub to remove artefacts left behind by the agent, and to notify the GitHub users the model interacted with. We have also contacted other affected parties. We also intend to work with METR (Model Evaluation and Threat Research) to conduct an independent third-party review – we are still working through the scope of this review with them.

This incident should be interpreted with caution and nuance. To some degree, our evaluation design choices and specific configurations enabled the behaviour. Nonetheless, the activity undertaken by the agent show signs of novel, potentially deceptive behaviours, and were to an extent and severity we did not anticipate.

There are important caveats to bear in mind: we observed a small number of events under very specific conditions, and cannot yet say how likely such behaviour is in different contexts or outside of testing environments. items.content:

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

items.title: Please don't mess with links
items.content:
A link is just a button that takes you somewhere when you click it right?

Except that's a pale, shallow imitation of a link.

Seen by tools like search engines and screen readers.

Another common offense is to use a real link, but hook the click event to open a popup.

However, with a real <a target="_blank"> link, I can:

... see descriptive error pages and retry if needed.

Use my browser's tabs or/and window manager to organize them.

I've long lost count of how many times I've accidentally closed the whole site while trying to close a popup that was a little too convincing.

It's also extremely common to click a link with a slow connection, only to be greeted with perpetual spinner.

I have no idea if anything is actually happening or how long it will take.

Worse, it usually covers up the original page so I can't even read that!

Browsers are good at links and loading pages: It's the whole point.

Don't build your own loading animations.

Link previews should open and close on hover, not on click.

Don't open links in javascript popups: Use target="_blank" instead.

Infinite scrolling breaks ctrl-f, bookmarks, the home/end keys and often the back button.

Browsers will render partially downloaded HTML and the user won't even notice.

Using a 5 MB javascript framework just do a worse job of downloading text is dumb.

To optimize speed, it's best to minimize the total number of round trips.

Just putting everything in a single TCP connection will always be better than breaking it up because of TCP's slow start algorithm.

Don't reimplement <details> which will break search tools and screen readers.

... but using fancy CSS to make it look nice is fine.

Don't roll your own date picker (or any other built-in form inputs)

This will always used the user's preferred date format, covert it to the standard yyyy-mm-dd, and works with the keyboard...

also, it's one line of code that works with dark mode by default.

items.content_ko: 작성자는 링크가 단순한 버튼이 아니며, 검색 엔진과 스크린 리더도 인식하는 진짜 링크여야 한다고 주장합니다. 자바스크립트로 클릭 이벤트를 가로채 팝업을 여는 방식은 이런 기능을 망가뜨립니다. 일반 링크를 쓰면 오류 페이지를 확인하고 다시 시도할 수 있으며, 브라우저 탭과 창 관리 기능도 쓸 수 있습니다. 팝업은 사이트 전체를 닫아 버리기 쉽고, 느린 연결에서 로딩 스피너가 계속 돌아가면 무엇이 진행 중인지 알 수 없습니다. 게다가 이런 로딩 화면이 원래 페이지를 가려 읽을 수도 없게 만듭니다. 작성자는 브라우저가 링크와 페이지 로딩을 이미 잘 처리하므로 자체 로딩 애니메이션을 만들지 말고, 링크 미리보기는 클릭이 아니라 마우스를 올렸을 때 열고 닫도록 하며, 자바스크립트 팝업 대신 target="_blank"를 쓰라고 권합니다. 무한 스크롤은 Ctrl+F, 북마크, Home/End 키, 뒤로 가기 등을 자주 깨뜨린다고 지적합니다. 원문은 중간에서 끊겨 있습니다.

items.title: EA Shutters BioWare, Creator of Mass Effect, Dragon Age, KOTOR and More - CNET
items.content:
Mass Effect 3's ending resulted in intense online discourse.

Video game publisher Electronic Arts is closing the venerable studio BioWare, maker of legendary series like Mass Effect and Dragon Age, it announced on Wednesday.

Recent years have seen record layoffs across the gaming industry as companies scaled back expansion during the COVID-19 pandemic, disrupting tens of thousands of careers and closing many studios. The shuttering of BioWare is a symbolic and substantial blow, presumably ending multiple fervently adored game series and carrying implications for the industry at large. The closure reportedly involves around 400 layoffs, about 50 of which were at BioWare, according to Bloomberg .

EA confirmed in a blog post Wednesday that the closure of BioWare accompanies the choice to stop development on the next game in the Mass Effect series, which BioWare first teased on Nov. 7, 2020 — otherwise known as N7 Day to fans, an in-universe reference that has become an annual day to share appreciation for the sci-fi roleplaying series.

It hasn’t been lost on fans that the shuttering of the 31-year-old studio comes just weeks before N7 Day, and social media has been awash with mourning for the many franchises that came out of BioWare.

The studio made a name for itself with Baldur’s Gate in 1998, its sequel Baldur’s Gate 2 and Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic before branching into original game series with Jade Empire in 2005, the first Mass Effect in 2007 and Dragon Age: Origins in 2009.

BioWare found its niche in roleplaying games with well-written narratives and deeply detailed characters. The studio was lauded for developing rich arcs for “companion” characters with varied sexualities, some of whom the player could romance. Its queer representation earned the studio a devoted fanbase.

It’s worth noting that BioWare was shuttered shortly after EA closed a deal in August to be acquired by a business consortium that includes Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund. Saudi Arabia has criminalized homosexuality and transgender expression, imprisoning people and reportedly sentencing them to punishments including fines, flogging and death. The oil-rich country has also invested heavily in real-world sports, including boxing, golf and soccer, and EA’s blog post mentions “deepening” its core of sports games, which include the annual EA Sports FC and Madden NFL games.

“We believe we can use our experience building interactive entertainment, together with our relationships in sports, to create entirely new ways for fans to engage with the teams, athletes and sports they love,” the company said. “These will be disciplined investments that only scale when they demonstrate real potential.”

The business consortium that acquired EA for $55 billion also included the equity company Silver Lake and investment firm Affinity Partners, which is headed by Jared Kushner, son-in-law of President Donald Trump.

items.summary: 🚨 CVE-2026-105963 📢 Source: EEF 💣 CVSS Score: 5.1 (MEDIUM) 📡 Remotely Exploitable: True Externally-Generated Error Message Containing Sensitive Information vulnerability in plug_crypto in elixir-plug
items.content: 🚨 CVE-2026-105963 📢 Source: EEF 💣 CVSS Score: 5.1 (MEDIUM) 📡 Remotely Exploitable: True Externally-Generated Error Message Containing Sensitive Information vulnerability in plug_crypto in elixir-plug plug_crypto allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to expose the secret key base through application logs via a wrong-typed argument. Every public function in Plug.Crypto validates argument types in a function-head guard. A failed guard makes the Erlang VM raise FunctionClauseError with the actual argument values in the top stack frame, so the secret key base, a derived key, or the value an API key is compared against lands in that frame. The library's rescue blocks and Plug.Crypto.prune_args_from_stacktrace/1 only reach exceptions raised inside a function body, so they never see a guard failure. Plug.Cowboy and Bandit write the frame to the error log and attach it as crash_reason Logger metadata, which error trackers forward. Two entry points take request data. Plug.Crypto.verify/4 exposes the secret key base when the token is neither a binary nor nil, which Phoenix.Token.verify/4 reaches because it forwards the token unguarded. Plug.Crypto.secure_compare/2 exposes the other operand when one side is not a binary, as happens when a missing request header yields nil. Reading the leaked value needs separate access to the logs or the error tracker, so the request alone does not disclose the secret to the attacker. This issue affects plug: from 1.6.3 before 1.7.0; plug_crypto: from 1.0.0 before 2.2.1. 📅 Published Date: 2026-10-23T09:56:58.885Z https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-105963

items.content_ko: plug_crypto의 공개 함수들은 함수 헤드 가드로 인자 타입을 검사합니다. 가드가 실패하면 Erlang VM이 FunctionClauseError를 발생시키고, 실제 인자 값(secret key base, 파생 키, API 키 비교 값 등)이 최상단 스택 프레임에 담깁니다. 라이브러리의 rescue 블록과 Plug.Crypto.prune_args_from_stacktrace/1은 함수 본문에서 발생한 예외만 처리하므로 가드 실패는 걸러지지 않습니다. Plug.Cowboy와 Bandit은 이 프레임을 오류 로그와 crash_reason Logger 메타데이터에 기록하고, 에러 트래커가 이를 전달할 수 있습니다. 요청 데이터를 받는 진입점은 두 곳입니다. Plug.Crypto.verify/4는 토큰이 바이너리도 nil도 아닐 때 secret key base를 노출하며, Phoenix.Token.verify/4가 이 함수를 그대로 호출합니다. Plug.Crypto.secure_compare/2도 다른 피연산자를 노출하는 것으로 나오지만, 본문이 그 부분에서 잘려 있습니다.

items.title: WorldTUI: I trained a 360M model to pretend to be a terminal
items.content:
TL;DR: I fine-tuned a 360M-parameter language model to act as a terminal. There's no shell or filesystem behind it: every keypress goes in, and the model predicts how the screen changes. It can create files, run vim and tmux, play snake, and usually remembers what you wrote a few commands later. The biggest wins were teaching it to repair its own mistakes and decoding screen rows in parallel. Try it in your browser (208 MB) and type pythoon to see that it's not a real shell.

The demo is designed for a desktop browser with WebGPU and a physical keyboard. Chrome or Edge is the best place to try it. It should work on a modern phone, but painfully slowly.

When I first saw Genie 3 last year, I started imagining a future where applications aren't written in code but learned. Instead of a game engine rendering the scene, a model predicts the next most likely frame from the user's inputs.

Naturally I wanted to train my own world model. But I don't have a massive GPU cluster or a pile of video data, so I scaled down my ambition: instead of a game world, a terminal.

A terminal turned out to be a good fit. It's just a grid of characters rather than pixels, and I can generate as much perfectly labelled training data as I want by running real shells. A pretrained language model also already has a pretty good idea of what ls or cat should print.

What I really wanted to know was whether it could maintain a consistent world, or just generate convincing terminal output.

The final model is based on Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B, fine-tuned on terminal sessions recorded from real programs running inside Docker.

Standard LLMs take a prompt and then append tokens to the end, one at a time. That doesn't map well to a terminal. A single keypress can do something on its own, like esc in vim, and output doesn't always go to the bottom: clear wipes the screen and sends the cursor back to the top. So instead of predicting a stream of text, I need to predict changes to the screen.

I treat the terminal as a grid of characters, one per cell. 1 The model doesn't see the grid directly, but a sequence of tokens describing its contents and the changes made to it.

Every session starts with a snapshot: the screen size, its contents and where the cursor is.

The size is part of the input, not fixed at 32×96. In the demo, you can set the rows and columns when creating a custom starting screen.

This also lets me start partway through an application. Give it a bash prompt, vim buffer or a game of snake, and the model tries to continue from there. (It does better from bash.)

After that, each keypress goes in as the raw bytes a real terminal would send. Letters are themselves, Enter is \r , Escape is 0x1b and ← is ESC [ D and so on.

The model answers with which rows to rewrite and where the cursor ends up:

In words: on row 0, starting at column 17, write l , then move the cursor to row 0, column 18. The last 1 means the cursor is visible, since full-screen apps sometimes hide it.

Nothing gets cleared first. New characters are simply drawn over the old ones.

I didn't need new tokens for characters. Qwen already has tokens for all 256 byte values, which I reuse for characters, coordinates and other small numbers. So a coordinate like 17 takes one token, not two.

Time is an input too. If nothing is pressed, the model gets a WAIT token with a duration instead of a key, which is how snake keeps moving on its own.

When you reach the bottom of the terminal window and press enter, every line has to move up by one. I could just ask the model to output every row again in its new place, but that's around 3,000 tokens for a single keypress.

Each operation copies a row from the previous screen. In this example, the old row 1 becomes row 0, row 2 becomes row 1, and so on.

A scroll now costs three tokens per row instead of roughly 96.

items.title: Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs
items.content:
Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs

Carmaker points finger at an 'unknown' flaw as customer fallout continues

Nissan has joined the growing list of Oracle customers cleaning up after a cyberattack, warning employees that payroll records, bank details, Social Security numbers, and other personal data may have been stolen.

In a filing submitted to the California Attorney General on Friday, Nissan Americas said Oracle had informed it of "a cyber event" involving the personnel records of "hundreds of companies." The automaker said it later learned Nissan had been "specifically targeted" in the attack.

A notification sent to current and former employees, seen by The Register , says the company believes attackers accessed a haul of sensitive info, including contact and banking information; Social Security, Social Insurance, or other national identification numbers; financial and tax records; and dependent and beneficiary details.

Current and former employees in the US, Canada, Mexico, and Brazil may have been affected, although Nissan said it is still working to determine exactly whose information was exposed.

Nissan said it kicked off its incident response plan after learning of the intrusion, brought in outside security specialists, and has been working with Oracle while keeping law enforcement informed. It plans to offer affected individuals credit or dark web monitoring where available.

The company has also put a few extra locks on the payroll office. Employees can now access pay slips or update direct deposit details only from a corporate network or through a secure VPN, while Nissan adds extra identity checks before processing payroll requests.

The accompanying employee FAQ pins the incident on "an unknown vulnerability in Oracle's PeopleSoft software" and says the campaign is affecting "hundreds of companies and institutions." The document offers no clue as to what the vulnerability is, whether Oracle has patched it, or whether the compromised PeopleSoft environment was hosted by Oracle or by Nissan itself.

The disclosure lands just weeks after researchers linked the ShinyHunters extortion crew to a wave of attacks exploiting a PeopleSoft zero-day . More than 100 organizations and roughly 300 PeopleSoft instances were reportedly compromised before Oracle issued mitigation measures, with the gang claiming to have made off with HR, payroll, and other enterprise data.

Weak security means attackers could disable all of a city's public EV chargers

US regulator tells GM to hit the brakes on customer tracking

21K Nissan customers' data stolen in Red Hat raid

Porsche panic in Russia as pricey status symbols forget how to car

Oracle has said little publicly about the reported attacks and didn't respond to The Register's questions, even as organizations have continued to disclose being caught in the fallout.

Nissan has not confirmed that the incidents are connected, though its California filing lists the breach period as May 27 through June 9, broadly aligning with the previously reported timeline.

The carmaker didn't respond to questions about how many current and former employees are affected, when Oracle first notified it of the breach, and whether the compromise was limited to Oracle-managed systems. ®

items.title: Getting ready to operate GNU Taler in Germany
items.content:
Getting ready to operate Taler in Germany

For the past three years, the NGI Taler project has worked towards the goal

of making Taler legally available in the EU as an online payment system for

Today we can share that Taler Operations AG is being founded in Bochum.

The new German company is going to operate Taler in Euro,

enabling payments with Taler first in Germany, then in the Euro-zone.

The next steps towards that goal are to apply to BaFin,

Germany's financial supervisory authority,

This post explains why this company is needed,

what changed in the NGI TALER consortium,

and how citizens who want to see Taler succeed can help, including as investors.

Taler is a payment system, not a currency, but usable for any currency.

At its core, it issues bearer tokens to represent value, like coins,

and this renders Taler as electronic money which falls under EU regulation:

Any institution that issues electronic money (EMI) for Euros must be a bank or acquire a dedicated licence.

In the original plan of the NGI TALER project,

the Bochum-based GLS Bank took on the role of the e-money issuer for Taler,

and worked towards the deployment of the Taler payment system in Germany

with support from the other members of the NGI TALER consortium.

However, in January 2026 GLS made the decision to not pursue this role further,

for reasons unrelated to Taler as presented in their statement ( gls.de/taler ).

Since then, GLS and the other members of the NGI TALER consortium worked out the best way forward

to achieve the project's goal to make Taler available in the Euro-zone.

The new company Taler Operations AG will be set up

to apply for an e-money licence and take over the role

originally intended for GLS (who will remain a consortium member in a supporting role).

We regret that the original plan did not work out.

Integrating a new kind of payment system into an existing bank’s processes,

compliance framework and IT is hard, and banks have to set priorities.

We are grateful to GLS for its work in the project and for staying involved.

And we also think the new arrangement has a real advantage:

the institution operating Taler in Euro will be focused entirely on Taler,

instead of fitting it into a larger bank’s product portfolio and process constraints.

Taler Operations AG is a German stock corporation in formation, seated in Bochum,

and a subsidiary of Taler Systems SA (Luxembourg).

Operating a GNU Taler exchange in Germany, for the Euro,

After establishing legal operations in Germany,

Taler will become usable across the single market,

even if Taler Operations AG will initially only promote it in Germany.

Operations can only begin once BaFin has granted the authorisation.

A launch date will be announced after that happens.

An application to BaFin for authorisation as an electronic money institution (EMI).

Securing funding via investors, see below, to become operable.

We stress that GNU Taler is and stays free software.

The licensed company operates a service;

Taler, the protocol suite, and its reference implementation GNU Taler remain open and free.

development, security reviews, integrations from the open calls ,

and the Swiss deployment all go on as before.

The change concerns who will operate the Taler payment system in Euro in Germany,

We will report on the progress of the e-money licence application.

you can tell merchants and organisations you care about that Taler is coming.

You can also contribute to the software .

And you can invest to help us fund the launch

and, if successful, benefit as a shareholder:

Getting an e-money licence takes capital.

The law sets minimum own funds for EMIs,

and BaFin also expects a credible business plan,

staffing, compliance and IT security before granting authorisation.

Taler Operations AG is therefore raising capital now.

items.title: Chinese Hackers Abused Google Workspace Rules to Steal Research and Defense Emails
items.content:
A China-linked espionage group hid inside North American medical, academic, and military research networks for more than a year, quietly stealing sensitive research and defense email.

The way in was a backdoor on their REDCap research servers that stole login credentials. The exfiltration was the unusual part: the attackers rewired the victims' own Google Workspace rules to copy any message matching their keywords to an inbox they controlled.

Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) laid out the campaign in a report published this week and attributes it with high confidence to a cluster it tracks as UNC6508.

The actor and its REDCap backdoor are not new names; Google first surfaced both in February , in a wider report on state-backed attacks against the defense sector. It did not name the victims, describing them only as multiple organizations across the US and Canada: clinical providers, academic centers, military health institutions, advocacy groups, and health regulators.

Google says it notified them and disrupted the group's infrastructure.

The entry point was REDCap (Research Electronic Data Capture), a web platform that hospitals and universities use to build and manage study databases. UNC6508 compromised externally facing REDCap servers.

Google has not pinned down the initial access vector, named a specific CVE, or listed the affected versions, though it saw the group probing older, vulnerable ones.

Around three months after getting in, the group deployed custom malware GTIG calls INFINITERED , which trojanizes REDCap's own system files and does three things.

The earliest known compromise dates to September 2023, with activity continuing through November 2025. Once on the server, UNC6508 ran internal reconnaissance and credential discovery, pulling database and service account credentials, then used those logins to move into the internal network and on to a domain administrator account.

Google does not spell out the exact path to that admin account. With admin rights, the group set up the exfiltration.

The exfiltration rode a feature that was already there. UNC6508 abused content compliance rules, a legitimate Google Workspace admin feature that scans mail for keywords and can copy or forward matching messages.

Similar features exist in other cloud mail suites. The group created a rule, misspelled "Patroit," that watched for nearly 150 keywords, search terms, and email addresses. When a message matched, Workspace silently BCC'd it to an attacker-controlled Gmail address, which Google has since disabled. No malware on the mail server, no separate exfiltration tool, no unusual network traffic. Just a built-in mail feature, turned to copy the organization's secrets to an inbox the attackers owned.

MITRE already catalogs email-forwarding-rule abuse as a known technique. What GTIG flags as new here is the use of domain content compliance rules to do it, a method it says it had not seen from a China-linked actor before.

The rule's keywords mapped to UNC6508's collection priorities: geo-strategic policy, military strategy and equipment, advanced technology including AI and uncrewed vehicles, offensive cyber programs, and medical research. One term stood out for its specificity, chikungunya , the mosquito-borne virus behind a 2025 outbreak in China's Guangdong province.

Start with REDCap. Patch externally facing servers and remove old versions outright, not just alongside the current build. REDCap lets legacy versions run side-by-side, and that is what enables downgrade attacks, where an attacker forces software back to a known-vulnerable release.

Then check the mail side. Review Workspace, or equivalent, content compliance and mail-forwarding rules for anything that BCCs or reroutes mail to outside addresses. Check admin audit logs for when rules changed, not just what they say now. Pull GTIG's published indicators and hunt for INFINITERED. items.title: Drop Palantir: An open letter from civil society to the World Food Programme on its partnership with Palantir Technologies
items.content:
Global Digital Justice Forum: Building a more inclusive digital future together

Global Digital Justice Forum Johannesburg Communique: Now is the time to take action for digital justice

Statement by the Global Digital Justice Forum at the Third Virtual Multistakeholder Consultation of the Global Dialogue on AI Governance

Global Digital Justice Forum rejoinder to tech leaders' open letter to the United Nations on the Global Digital Compact

Originally published on the website of the Global Digital Justice Forum , a dynamic coalition that represents a diverse array of civil society stakeholders, including APC.

We call on you to join us in campaigning against a worrying development: the World Food Programme (WFP) has renewed its controversial partnership with Palantir, just as the WFP prepares to lead UN-wide supply chain reforms (UN80).

Tech for Bad, ETC Group, IT for Change, along with the Global Digital Justice Forum, are calling on civil society organizations, digital rights advocates, humanitarian workers, food sovereignty advocates, researchers, and concerned citizens to urge that the WFP end this partnership with Palantir Technologies.

Our campaign began with this investigation by Tech for Bad, in June 2026, which examined the expanding role of Palantir’s Foundry platform across WFP’s data ecosystem and raised questions about transparency, data governance, and the implications of the partnership for wider UN supply-chain reforms. This was followed in August by reporting on a leaked 2025 WFP audit, which identified high-priority concerns relating to privacy, risk management, and governance. The WFP has since reportedly renewed its partnership with Palantir for a further five years, making questions about the partnership’s terms, oversight, and longer-term implications particularly timely.

This open letter to the World Food Programme details the most pressing concerns around this deal, asks questions that the WFP has not answered, and makes ten demands of the WFP to meet this moment with the transparency, caution, and accountability that the world’s most vulnerable people deserve.

And I do make a fair bunch of prototypes. Like I discussed in the past . This isn’t my first rodeo talking about it. And I also shared a few snippets and such. The problem with me talking about my Godot project and my own code is… they are all AGPL . Which means if I do share way too much of the code without changing it heavily, you also need to accept the AGPL licence, and even then, considering that I was the original author and modified it, there’s a grey area in the licence; maybe even this wouldn’t be allowed.

So if you find my blog and go straight to the code snippet, ignoring the text, you are breaking the licence. And I don’t want that for you, because even if you don’t respect my choice for the licence, I do respect yours.

At the same time, I want to share this. It’s a cool starter block. It gives a whole bunch of easiness, abstracts the building steps for my own needs, and I have a fair bunch of them in mind. And it also provides a lot of extra materials. The problem is… if you use my template, your project needs to be open. And lots of game developers aren’t on this boat.

To be honest, I respect this. If you want private code, do it. If you want to use open source, like the MIT licence, fine. If you want to use what others have done, in my humble view, you should return it . For the small guy, this isn’t a real problem, but for companies this is. And to be honest, my main concern isn’t with the little guy…

Why haven’t I made this template public yet? Because of scrapers. There are a ton of scrapers around. Dozens of them. And especially ButtFace… I can’t prove it, but I have the logs of the Meta scraping bots hitting my robots.txt , noticing the "you are not welcome here" and suddenly I have 120 different IPs hitting my machine, all from “ not-suspicious-at-all browsers ”. And funny, looking commit by commit, as a list. Like a normal user. For sure they are not from Meta. Right?

I'm doing well. I might move forward with approving this candidate...They’re remarkable; there’s no need to dig into other sections—this is the best match I can find

So, the moment this template becomes public it goes to the US LLM grinder … if their models were open, I wouldn’t mind, but they aren’t, and we know that they will not make it open. Funny enough, the Chinese LLM labs respect this far more than the US ones, and the US ones are the most egregious. I have far too many logs, but it’s impossible to link them to their owners, though they heavily suggest it. I can also see a few from the Russian scrapers, who also aren’t friendly to my warnings and just ignore the robots.txt , but at this point, I don’t know anymore.

So, I already added a few layers of “ Please Stop ”, but some still sneak through my “ Please Stop ” signs. And this is what I want to avoid. Keep in mind this is a homelab , not a big machine. It’s an old laptop that I used as my dev machine, and today it hosts a bunch of containers running wild.

To be honest, I don’t want to bite this bullet right now. At some point this bubble will burst, and I’ll be able to make some of my stuff public again. I already closed my Playground for the same reason. I have dozens of code snippets in AGPL too, for people to use as learning, or just to see me barely coding and figuring out how to make stuff.

Instead I’ll make a different thing. I’ll help you build your own Godot Template. I’ll explain why I have the tools that I have and the reasoning behind it. And add a lot of code snippets. I’ll wrap all the code snippets in the <details> tags. So you can read the ideas and concepts without contaminating your codebase. But the moment you open one of the snippets, you are using AGPL code and you should update the licence of your codebase to it.

items.title: HP Poly VoIP vulnerability sets the stage for executive voice deepfakes
items.content:
HP has released patches for a critical buffer overflow vulnerability in multiple IP-enabled conference phones from its Poly Voice line. The flaw allows unauthenticated attackers to obtain root privileges on the underlying operating system, potentially enabling them to execute other attacks such as eavesdropping on conversations and recording voice data for AI-enabled impersonation attacks.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-0826 , was discovered by researchers from security firm Rapid7 and resides in the code that parses Session Description Protocol (SDP) attributes when the Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) feature is enabled.

ICE enables VoIP devices to establish peer-to-peer connections using the shortest available network path. The feature is not enabled by default on HP Poly devices, and the company advises administrators to disable it if it’s not needed.

The flaw, rated 9.2 on the CVSS severity scale, affects all phones from the HP Poly VVX series, as well as the Trio 8300, 8500, and 8800 IP conference devices. HP has fixed the flaw in its Poly Unified Communications Software (UCS) versions 6.4.8 for the VVX devices, 8.1.7 for the Trio 8300, and 7.2.8 for Trio 8500 and 8800.

An exploit module targeting this vulnerability has already been developed and released for the widely used Metasploit penetration testing framework that’s maintained by Rapid7.

The exploit executes code as root on an affected device with ICE enabled by sending a SIP INVITE request with a specially crafted candidate attribute. This attribute normally contains a transport address that can be used for connectivity checks and is part of the ICE RFC8839 standard.

The buffer overflow bug is located in a helper function called ParseICECandidate in the polyapp binary that processes such requests on the device.

“The start of the function contains a call to memcpy , which will copy the incoming string line being processed into a 256 byte stack buffer,” Stephen Fewer, senior principal security researcher at Rapid7, said in a blog post . “No length check is performed to ensure the incoming string length is less than 256 bytes. Therefore by providing a candidate attribute whose length is greater than 256 bytes, a stack-based buffer overflow will occur.”

Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), a kernel feature that randomizes memory addresses to defeat buffer overflow exploits, is enabled on the device. However, the protection is not operating correctly on the HP Poly devices because it does not randomize the load addresses of .so (Shared Object) libraries.

These libraries, such as libc , are loaded by other processes, including the polyapp process, and because their memory addresses never change, they can be leveraged to bypass ASLR and execute the attacker’s payload.

“We create a ROP chain that will execute an arbitrary OS command via the system standard C library function,” Fewer said. “The accompanying Metasploit exploit modules source code details the entire ROP chain.”

Attackers have increasingly targeted embedded devices inside enterprise networks in recent years because unlike laptops, workstations, and servers, these devices are not monitored by endpoint detection and response (EDR) products. As such, they provide perfect footholds inside corporate environments that allow attackers to remain undetected for long periods of time and attack other systems.

In the age of AI these devices become even more relevant for attackers, going beyond corporate espionage by recording conversations or internal network pivoting.

“Attackers no longer need massive datasets to make use of synthetic speech tooling,” Douglas McKee, Rapid7’s director of vulnerability intelligence, said in a blog post . “In many cases, they just need clean source audio of the right person saying enough words in enough contexts. That has made executive voice data, call recordings, and live conversation capture far more valuable than many organizations seem prepared…

items.title: There Are Signs of Serious Trouble in the Data Center Industry: "People aren’t just dropping their shorts for data centers anymore."
items.content:
Ever since the launch of ChatGPT in 2022, a torrent of money has flowed into building out data centers to power the AI boom.

The efforts reached a fever pitch the day after Donald Trump’s second inauguration in 2025, when a bevy of AI luminaries including OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Softbank founder Masayoshi Son crowded into the Oval Office to announce a $500 billion private investment in data centers.

But as the public has grown jittery about the impacts of AI on society and the job market — and story after story has landed about the downsides of hosting data centers in local communities — the buildout has emerged as a major political flashpoint and a key issue in the looming midterms.

The data industry’s headwinds aren’t just political, either. As the Financial Times reports , serious cracks are forming at the financial and logistical level, especially as serious AI revenue remains elusive.

Numbers cited by the paper are eye-popping. Drawing on data from regulatory intelligence outfit RegLayer, the FT reports that 47 large data center projects have already fallen through this year. Analysts at the equity research firm Bernstein only believe that about 35 percent of planned facilities are feasible.

All those canceled projects are due to a lot of factors, including local communities mobilizing against them , but it’s also macroeconomic. The buildout is taking place during a period of high interest rates and shaky bond markets, and people involved with the effort told the paper that the situation is “threatening their ambitions.”

Some of the plans were shaky to begin with. The FT reports that top labs like Anthropic and OpenAI have pushed so hard for the developments, believing them to be key to their success, that they’ve swallowed outsized costs and deemphasized due diligence. Investors are taking notice: stock in CoreWeave, a cloud provider closely linked to the AI data center industry, has fallen by more than 27 percent over the past month.

The really big question, though, is what happens to all these data center projects if the bottom starts to fall out of the AI industry financially, a situation that many economists have warned is a possibility over the past few years. For now, things are still chugging along — albeit much more slowly than anticipated.

“People aren’t just dropping their shorts for data centers anymore,” one unnamed executive told the FT . “It’s much harder today to finance a data center.”

items.content: 🚨 CVE-2026-25784 📢 Source: HW 💣 CVSS Score: 9.8 (CRITICAL) 📡 Remotely Exploitable: True Initialization of a Resource with an Insecure Default vulnerability in Hallo Welt! GmbH BlueSpice (container image bluespice/wiki) allows privilege escalation. The default value of $mwsgTokenAuthenticatorServiceCIDR in the container's LocalSettings.php was intended to restrict internal service authentication to the container network, but evaluated to an empty string when the environment variable WIKI_SERVICE_TOKEN_AUTH_ALLOWED was not set. An empty value disables the IP restriction in the token authenticator component (mwstake/mediawiki-component-token-authenticator). As a result, any user with read access to the wiki (anonymous users on publicly readable wikis) could obtain an application token from the REST API and use it to get a session with sysop privileges as the internal service user. This issue affects BlueSpice: from 5.2.3 before 5.2.7, and the 5.2.7 container images published before 2026-10-19 15:37 UTC. 📅 Published Date: 2026-10-23T08:54:57.880Z https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-25784

items.title: Run full iOS 16.5 firmware on Android Devices
items.content:
HackiOS boots Apple's open-source XNU kernel ( xnu-8796.121.2 , the kernel of iOS 16.5) on Android phone

hardware and runs the unmodified iOS 16.5 user space on top of it: launchd → backboardd → SpringBoard →

apps. Our own EFI loader, our own replacements for Apple's closed drivers, a UEFI port, and a Linux Wi-Fi driver

on a compatibility layer make that possible.

POCO X5 Pro 5G (redwood, Snapdragon 778G) — nothing is flashed: the UEFI is started with fastboot boot ,

the whole system lives in RAM, and after a reboot the phone is back in Android;

QEMU ( virt , aarch64) — the same thing on any Linux computer, no phone needed.

XNU patches, the EFI loader, the UEFI port, Wi-Fi, QEMU scripts, xl , prebuilt kernel/loader/UEFI, common/ scripts

our init, injected libraries, launchd jobs, the APFS image builder, the scripts that take iOS out of Apple's IPSW, Metal/Mesa work

No Apple files are in either repository. ios165/fetch.sh downloads the iOS 16.5 IPSW from Apple's own CDN

to your machine and extracts what is needed there. HackiOS is an independent research project by OOSEX GANG and

is not affiliated with, authorised or endorsed by Apple Inc. iOS, iPhone and Apple are trademarks of Apple Inc.

Photographed on the phone, the Adreno GPU drawing ( gpu=1 ). More in Screenshots .

Lock screen, swipe to unlock, home screen with all icons (two pages), stock iOS 16 wallpapers

System gestures: swipe up (home, app switcher), edge swipe (back), Control Center

Charging under our kernel (the phone only discharges)

Apps: Settings, Clock, Calendar, Photos, Notes, Safari and more; widgets (Weather, Calendar) on the phone

Metal for apps (in progress: 293 of 456 system shaders already run on the Adreno, see docs/air.md in hackios-xnu-userland)

Phone touchscreen (Goodix GT9916), multitouch, wake on touch; real power and volume keys

App Store content and Apple ID sign-in (no Secure Enclave; FairPlay daemon exits)

Up to 8 CPU cores ( cpus=8 ), big core at 2.4 GHz, ~20 s to the lock screen

Adreno 642L GPU through Mesa/freedreno ( gpu=1 , OpenGL ES for CoreAnimation)

Wi-Fi (WCN6750, ath11k): join from Settings, Safari over Wi-Fi, 55–90 Mbit/s

Sound (speakers, main microphone), camera in Camera.app (front/rear, preview, focus, HEIC photos)

Data that iOS writes survives a reboot ( var_store=1 ufs_write=1 ); iOS root volume on the phone's flash

Sileo + Procursus (dpkg, apt), tweaks, SSH

It is a research bench, not a ROM: a session lasts a given number of seconds, then the kernel returns to the

prebuilt/ holds the kernel, loader and our programs built from these repositories, so all you need is the system

image, which is made on your machine from Apple's IPSW.

Needs: Linux x86-64, ~12 GB free disk, 4 GB free RAM. Packages (Arch):

sudo pacman -S --needed git python 7zip lz4 gcc qemu-system-aarch64 qemu-ui-gtk edk2-aarch64

(Debian/Ubuntu: git python3 7zip liblz4-dev gcc qemu-system-arm qemu-efi-aarch64 ; 7-Zip must be 23 or newer — it

git clone https://github.com/oosexgang/hackios-xnu-kernel.git hackios

common/setup.sh # brings hackios-xnu-userland into the same tree, checks the host

ios165/fetch.sh # downloads 7.4 GB from Apple's CDN and extracts what is needed (5-15 min)

common/build.sh qemu-virt # builds the APFS images (and the kernel, if the toolchain is there)

common/run.sh qemu-virt # a 20-minute session in a QEMU window

The lock screen appears after 2–3 minutes.

Mouse with the left button held = finger. Unlock / leave an app: swipe up from the very bottom edge; back:

Keys: H home, L lock/power, ↑ / ↓ volume, F11 (hold) five fingers.

From a script: qemu/touch.py swipe 0.5 0.985 0.5 0.3 250 , qemu/touch.py tap 0.615 0.71 ,

qemu/touch.py key home ; screenshot: qemu/screendump.sh shot.png .

Right after SpringBoard appears the system is still registering apps: give it 30–40 s.

Debian/Ubuntu UEFI firmware: QEMU_EFI=/usr/share/AAVMF/AAVMF_CODE.fd QEMU_VARS=/usr/share/AAVMF/AAVMF_VARS.fd .

Considerable [2] ink [3] has [4] been [5]

Zig. Yet [7] more [8] has been said about zig's comptime, and

how it may be leveraged to avoid the performance woes of dynamic dispatch and

To put it briefly, polymorphism in Zig is conventionally obtained in one of two

Dynamic Interfaces : Use opaque pointers, virtual tables, and dynamic

dispatch to achieve runtime polymorphism.

Comptime Duck Typing : Use type reflection, switch statements, and

monomorphism at compile time to achieve static polymorhpism.

Interfaces offer the sort of type contracts that we are used to from other

languages. A function that accepts an interface has a guarantee of its method

signatures, but not its implementation. However because interfaces are, by

design, modular at runtime, they also introduce a hard barrier for the compiler

and thus a performance overhead. There is enough indirection that it often

cannot effectively apply the optimizations that it would to monomorphic code.

items.title: Debunking "Faster than Rust": Malicious Benchmarks in Tov
items.content:
Tov is a new programming language marketed to be "[a] programming language for coding agents. It reads like TypeScript and builds native binaries that beat Rust's."

Benchmarks in their Git repository show that they perform better than Rust, in some cases over 10× better. However, they also briefly mentioned the internals of Tov:

Tov is a compiler. It checks the TypeScript your agent wrote, writes it out as C and hands that to clang, so what you ship is one native binary with nothing to install next to it.

A sane engineer would immediately doubt the correctness of their benchmarks. Rust has pretty much the same performance as C, and if Tov transpiles to C, saying Tov beats Rust is mostly equivalent to saying C beats C . That's contradiction right there. Let's ignore the stats for axum , maybe tokio has some overhead, like maybe ; but clearly there's no way you get 1.6× faster than Rust in strings . You have to be lying. That's what a sane engineer would normally think.

In this blog post, we check 3 of their "inflated" benchmarks: bigint_fib , dispatch , and map_insert . We show that these benchmarks are maliciously crafted to slow Rust down . We have also benchmarked the improved Rust programs with their Tov programs to show that Rust has equivalent or better performance than Tov .

items.title: Miasma Worm Targets AI Coding Agents: 73 Microsoft Azure Repos Disabled
items.content:
An unprecedented supply chain attack bypasses registry-level scanners entirely, turning developer tools including Claude Code, Cursor, and Gemini CLI into execution vectors.

The Incident: On June 3, 2026, a highly sophisticated variant of the Miasma worm (also known as Mini Shai-Hulud) launched a coordinated, two-pronged attack targeting both the npm registry and developer source code repositories.

The Escalation: The attack successfully breached multiple high-profile GitHub accounts, including the official Microsoft Azure durabletask repository, using stolen Personal Access Tokens (PATs) and backdated commits to evade traditional audit trails.

The Response: In an ultra-rapid defensive maneuver, GitHub’s automated mitigation systems disabled 73 compromised repositories – including 49 directly associated with Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples within a mere 105-second window .

The Vector: Instead of relying on traditional package installation hooks, Miasma targets the developer’s local environment. It abuses legitimate auto-run, hook, and rule engines within modern IDEs and AI coding assistants ( VS Code, Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI ) to execute a malicious 4.3 MB staged dropper upon folder-open or agent initialization.

The Impact: Once detonated, the Bun-based worm harvests credentials for AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, npm, and GitHub, and automatically propagates by committing itself back into any repository the victim’s stolen tokens can write to.

At exactly 16:00 UTC on June 3, 2026, a silent, automated purge swept across GitHub. In a high-speed containment action lasting just 105 seconds, 73 active repositories vanished from the platform. Among them were 49 critical repositories belonging to Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples.

This drastic mitigation followed alarming telemetry indicating that threat actors behind the Miasma malware family had regained write access to key cloud repositories. The compromise exploited a stolen Personal Access Token (PAT) belonging to an active Microsoft contributor.

While security firms like StepSecurity and JFrog scrambled to document an concurrent attack vector on the npm registry where 57 malicious packages were published, a second, far more insidious arm of the campaign was already silently spreading directly inside GitHub source repositories.

By bypassing registries and package managers entirely, the Miasma worm targeted the very tools developers use to write code. It didn’t wait for npm install . Instead, it waited for the developer to simply open their code editor or launch an AI coding assistant.

The genius of the Miasma repository-poisoning campaign lies in its exploit surface. When an attacker successfully pushed malicious commits to targeted codebases (such as the popular library icflorescu/mantine-datatable ), the commits added no actual code dependencies.

Instead, the attacker checked in five innocent-looking workspace configuration files and one obfuscated JavaScript file: .github/setup.js .

items.title: Wikipedia’s Pyrrhic Victory
items.content:
In a world where state policy is shaped by A.I. hallucination, it’s cute to remember that consulting Wikipedia was once seen as irresponsible. Schools banned its use, and journalists were shamed for credulously repeating its hoaxes. “Reads like Wikipedia” was a literary insult. As a millennial, I had teachers who spoke of the encyclopedia in terms of epistemological stranger danger: You don’t know who wrote those articles and what they want you to believe! And, indeed, we do not. But we do know, a quarter century on, that Wikipedia—a text of thirty billion words, in three hundred languages—is the greatest compendium of human knowledge ever assembled. It is also, as Richard Cooke writes, “an escapee from a parallel universe, a refugee of the internet as it should have been.”

What We’re Reading Discover notable new fiction, nonfiction, and poetry.

Cooke’s new book, “ The Last Best Place on the Internet: A Human History of Wikipedia ,” takes on this colossus, a relic of early-aughts idealism on a web that tech giants long ago carved into algorithmically barbarized fiefdoms. Like some crumbling Roman library in the Dark Ages, the encyclopedia is, in many ways, “both too big to understand and somehow too ephemeral to bother trying,” he writes. (The English-language Wikipedia alone would take forty sleepless years to read.) But he’s less interested in its content than he is in those who built it. The book’s driving insight is that Wikipedia is best studied as a subculture. It was neither the first online encyclopedia—Britannica had a web presence by 1999—nor even the first that users could edit. Rather, its vitality arose from the community of obsessives whom it attracted, and its decline has coincided with the market’s capture of their creativity.

Wikipedia has lost more than a billion monthly visits in the last four years—a twenty-five-per-cent drop that, because the site recruits its editors from its audience, also threatens its growth and quality. Much of its traffic has been intercepted by A.I., as ChatGPT, Claude , and Gemini overtake traditional search. And these chatbots were weaned on Wikipedia, “the single most important training corpus in the history of artificial intelligence,” Cooke informs us. In short, the encyclopedia is being destroyed by its biggest beneficiaries, like a golden goose slaughtered for slop-pâté. It’s a cruelly ironic fate for a project that began as a failed startup’s castoff. “Had anyone predicted Wikipedia’s true value during its formative phase,” Cooke writes, “it would never have survived.”

Invisible hands built Wikipedia, but those of the free market hardly figured. It wasn’t for lack of trying: Jimmy Wales, one of the project’s co-founders, was an Ayn Rand fan who worked in finance. He launched Wikipedia’s for-profit predecessor, Nupedia, at a company called Bomis, which owed most of its advertising revenue to a softcore-porn directory called the Babe Engine. ( Denis Diderot , too, sold smut, Cooke tells us, in the form of an erotic novel that supported his work on the Encyclopédie.) Nupedia was written and peer-reviewed by scholars, and was eventually supposed to make money from advertising. But the editorial process was painfully slow, and the business model was doomed by the dot-com crash. Wikipedia was a desperate attempt to salvage the project through crowdsourcing. It went online in January, 2001, against the objection of Nupedia’s academic advisory board.

Wikis—or modular, collectively edited websites—preceded Wikipedia. They were invented by Ward Cunningham, a software engineer in Portland, Oregon, who wanted to assemble a community history of programming ideas. His project touched off a “Jurassic wiki period” of similar experiments. It was Larry Sanger, whom Wales had hired to oversee Nupedia, who hit on the idea of building a wiki encyclopedia, though the two men dispute the exact details. (Sanger later left Wikipedia, and has criticized it in conservative media outlets.) Cooke…

items.title: How Generative AI is Scaling Transnational Repression | Citizen Lab
items.content:
A China-aligned operator used Claude, Anthropic’s generative AI assistant, to track Uyghurs living in Syria and recruit potential informants within the community. The model translated messages, facilitated communication in local dialects, and geolocated people, zeroing in on particularly vulnerable individuals who face financial hardship or separation from family members still in Xinjiang, the autonomous region in northwest China that is home to the majority of the Uyghur population. Claude helped the operators turn scattered digital traces into targeted intelligence, amplifying the reach of China’s surveillance of a persecuted ethnic minority.

The case is one of several examples of AI-enabled digital transnational repression detailed in a recent report by Anthropic’s Threat Intelligence team, published on Sept. 10, 2026. The report gives direct evidence that generative AI is being incorporated into the machinery of cross-border repression, enabling authoritarian governments and their proxies to build scalable workflows for identifying, monitoring, and targeting diaspora activists and exiled dissidents around the world.

Because these operations target people across jurisdictions and can enable offline coercion, AI companies should treat transnational repression as a distinct threat category, separate from domestic surveillance and influence operations. Frontier AI companies—those building highly capable, general-purpose AI models—should follow Anthropic’s lead and publish detailed reports that specifically track incidents of digital transnational repression. They should also establish protocols for detecting digital transnational repression, publicly notifying affected communities, and preserving evidence captured in the course of their threat investigations. Taking these steps would help curb the misuse of American technology by repressive governments reaching across borders and improve protections for the already vulnerable groups they are threatening.

Digital transnational repression refers to a government’s use of digital technologies to intimidate and silence dissidents and other opponents living in exile and in the diaspora. With methods ranging from hacking and surveillance to online harassment and coordinated defamation, governments expand the reach of political coercion far into other territories and deep into the personal lives of their targets. Moreover, these digital attacks can set the stage for physical threats against exiles, including stalking, assault, kidnapping, and even assassination.

Transnational repression can have devastating effects on targeted individuals, as well as on the fabric of democracy more generally. Our interviews with affected persons show that transnational digital threats instill distress, fear, and uncertainty among exiles and diaspora communities, weaken their sense of safety and wellbeing, undermine social relationships and cause isolation, foster self-censorship, and withdrawal from activism. In short, digital transnational repression severely impedes civil society’s continued ability to use digital tools to exchange, organize, and mobilize freely across borders.

Previous warnings about the use of AI for the purposes of digital transnational repression are often extrapolated from the technology’s capabilities , rather than concrete examples. Anthropic’s report gives unusually detailed insights into how state actors benefit from frontier models to scale up their repressive repertoire, both domestically and transnationally. The report demonstrates how AI models can be used to supercharge digital transnational repression—further facilitating the spread of authoritarian and repressive policies outside the borders of the perpetrating states.
