items.title: OpenShell – A safe, private runtime for fleets of autonomous AI agents
items.content:
New in OpenShell 0.1.x: a stable release cadence, new isolation primitives, an expanded extension surface, and new APIs. Read the 0.1.0 upgrade guide .

OpenShell is the safe, private runtime for fleets of autonomous AI agents. Agents are most useful when they can read files, install packages, call APIs, and use credentials. OpenShell gives them that capability without giving them unrestricted access to your data, secrets, or network. You declare what each agent can touch in a policy, and OpenShell enforces it.

OpenShell governs what agents can do in two ways: it instruments the kernel to enforce policy on every file access, system call, and network connection at runtime, and it uses formal verification to check what a policy change would allow before it is applied.

Kernel-level enforcement. Each agent runs in an isolated sandbox. Kernel controls confine which files it can access and which system calls it can make, and every network connection passes through a policy check before it leaves the sandbox. Agents never see real credentials; OpenShell adds them only to requests bound for approved endpoints.

Formally verified policy changes. Before a policy change is approved, OpenShell uses formal verification to flag risky new access it would grant, such as reaching a new host with credentials or calling a new API method, so those changes wait for human review.

See Architecture for how the gateway, supervisor, and sandbox fit together.

You need Linux, macOS on Apple Silicon, or Windows with WSL 2 (experimental), plus Docker, Podman, or host virtualization. See the Support Matrix for details.

curl -LsSf https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NVIDIA/OpenShell/main/install.sh | sh

The installer sets up the CLI and a local gateway. The default sandbox image is minimal Ubuntu with no agent installed. To run a real agent, follow Run Your First Agent : it runs OpenCode against a free OpenRouter model and shows how to approve new access as the agent needs it.

Sandboxes : images, runtimes, GPUs, and lifecycle.

Policies : filesystem, network, and process rules, with the advisor and prover for reviewing changes.

Providers : credentials that work only at approved endpoints, including inference .

Gateways : the control plane for sandboxes, policy, and access.

Kubernetes : deploy the gateway with Helm. Your CNI must enforce NetworkPolicy .

Extensibility : middleware, interceptors, and compute drivers.

Tutorials : step-by-step policy and agent walkthroughs.

Prerelease and development builds : try an upcoming release or the latest commit on main .

Install the public OpenShell skills for your coding agent:

The skills teach your agent to drive the OpenShell CLI, write sandbox policies, and debug gateways and inference routing. They live in skills/ and work without an OpenShell source checkout.

SDKs connect applications to an OpenShell gateway. They do not install the CLI. Use the same OpenShell release for the SDK and the gateway when possible.

npm install @nvidia/openshell-sdk (GitHub Packages)

go get github.com/NVIDIA/OpenShell/sdk/go@latest

cargo add openshell-sdk --git https://github.com/NVIDIA/OpenShell --tag <release-tag>

Questions and discussion: GitHub Discussions

Bug reports and feature requests: GitHub Issues , using the issue templates

Security vulnerabilities: follow SECURITY.md . Do not open a GitHub issue.

Roadmap: OpenShell Roadmap and the RFC board

OpenShell is built agent-first: it is developed with the same agent-driven workflows it enables. See CONTRIBUTING.md for development setup and the contribution workflow, and AGENTS.md for repository coding conventions.

OpenShell collects anonymous telemetry, limited to operational categories and counts, to help improve the project. It does not collect sandbox names, hostnames, file paths, prompts, credentials, provider or model names, or user content. To disable it, set OPENSHELL_TELEMETRY_ENABLED=false on the gateway, or server.telemetryEnabled=false for Helm…

I started with Tailwind, but got annoyed of the workflow of having to find out what the Tailwind equivalent of a given CSS rule is and what the allowed values are. items.title: Lawsuits Can’t Restrain Big Tech
items.content:
W hen the government first filed major antitrust lawsuits targeting Big Tech back in 2020, many people were optimistic that the long-standing practice of public legal action against monopolistic companies could rein in these economy-dominating corporations.

But as these pages have covered , this “techlash” has come to little. Antitrust law has conformed to its castrated character of recent decades, with the state unable to bring itself to seriously restrain, let alone break up, the giant companies even after they were ruled to be full monopolies just months before.

Recently, when it comes to enforcing the law against the tech giants, new lows have been reached.

G oogle’s first antitrust suit concerned its control of web search, and it was ruled to have operated a monopoly yet was given only a slap on the wrist. Rather than being broken up or forced to sell off any of its major corporate units like Chrome, the court imposed rather toothless “behavioral” remedies, barring exclusive default-search deals and requiring the company to share some search data with rivals.

A second case was brought by the Department of Justice in 2023 over Google’s “ad tech” business, an industry term referring to the segment of the company’s ad business that helps independent websites (such as news publishers) sell ads on their own pages. Google owns what are by far the dominant tools for this market, including the exchange itself (known as AdX) where advertisers find publishers as well as the servers that deliver the ad content. The company charges a 20 percent fee to run ad auctions for websites, which occur in fractions of a second as your browser opens the webpage in question.

It should be said at the outset that ad tech is a small part of Google — the $30 billion in revenue it brought in for 2025 comes to just 7 percent of Alphabet’s total revenue, and that share has been in decline for years. The Justice Department wanted the court to force Google to sell off AdX.

The judge’s full opinion remained under seal for weeks while both sides were given the chance to redact confidential information from it. The now-revealed remedies include a requirement for Google to make its ad exchange interoperable with competitors, meaning that using Google’s marketplace for finding bidders wouldn’t lock publishers into using its other tools. It also forces the company to share some real-time bidding data with publishers.

But unsurprisingly, in Google’s second monopolist verdict in two years, the company was still not subjected to any form of breakup. Judge Leonie M. Brinkema found such a measure to be “neither realistic nor needed.” Instead she settled for narrower measures such as those mentioned above as well as obliging Google to retain a court-appointed monitor with limited power over the firm. The “remedies” will stay in place for only six years , rather than the fifteen years that the government sought. And Google of course plans to appeal the finding of monopolization, which will take some years.

The company is now an adjudicated monopolist twice over, but the liberal state has failed to even partially rewrite Alphabet.

M eanwhile, the private arm of the techlash appears to be producing more serious consequences. Years of attempts by litigants to sue the platforms for their harmful content have failed, due to strong legal protections shielding the companies for material posted by users. But more recently, users have hit on the legal argument that the designs of the platforms themselves are harmful, and intentionally so.

Reporting and disclosures about such design choices have bolstered these cases, from the Wall Street Journal in its damning “Facebook Files” series that drew on leaked internal Meta research to company documents unsealed in court. items.title: Regexp compilation fixes related to GitLab's CVE-2026-89078, CVE-2026-93577, CVE-2026-97229 and CVE-2026-110264
items.content:
Regexp compilation fixes related to GitLab's CVE-2026-89078, CVE-2026-93577, CVE-2026-97229 and CVE-2026-110264

We have released Ruby 4.0.9, 3.4.12 and 3.3.13. They fix several bugs in Ruby’s regular expression engine (Onigmo) that GitLab found could be used for remote code execution on GitLab servers. GitLab published four CVEs for these issues, and the Ruby releases contain the fixes for the underlying bugs in Ruby.

GitLab compiles regular expressions supplied by its users, such as patterns in CI configuration, with Regexp.new . GitLab found that specially crafted patterns could corrupt memory while Ruby compiles them, and that this could be turned into remote code execution on GitLab servers. GitLab addressed these issues in its own releases by patching the Ruby it ships, and assigned the following CVE identifiers:

CVE-2026-89078 : Double Free issue in Regular Expression Parser ( GitLab 19.4.1 )

CVE-2026-93577 : Integer Overflow issue in Regular Expression Compiler ( GitLab 19.4.1 )

CVE-2026-97229 : Integer Overflow issue in CI/CD Regular Expression Compiler ( GitLab 19.4.2 )

CVE-2026-110264 : Integer Overflow issue in Regular Expression Compiler ( GitLab 19.5.1 )

The following table shows the change in Ruby that fixes the bug behind each CVE, and the first release of each series that contains it.

Double free when parsing a pattern fails after an alternation

Integer overflow in the size of a compiled pattern

Overflow of internal IDs in a pattern with many repeats

Ruby 4.0.9, 3.4.12 and 3.3.13 contain all of these fixes.

These bugs are reached only when an application compiles a regular expression from a string that an attacker controls, for example by passing it to Regexp.new , Regexp.union or Regexp.compile , or by interpolating it into a regexp literal such as /#{input}/ . Applications that only use regular expressions written by their own developers are not affected.

Regexp.timeout does not protect against these bugs. Limiting the length of patterns does not reliably protect against them either, because some of them can be triggered by short patterns.

We recommend upgrading to Ruby 4.0.9, 3.4.12 or 3.3.13 or later.

If you cannot upgrade, please avoid compiling regular expressions from untrusted input.

Ruby 3.3 is in the security maintenance phase, in which we normally release only fixes for vulnerabilities. Ruby 3.3.13 includes these fixes as an exception, because GitLab assigned CVEs to issues that rely on them.

We have not requested CVE identifiers in Ruby for these fixes, at least for now.

Ruby has generally considered it unsafe to compile and use a regular expression created from untrusted input. We stated this in the advisory for CVE-2022-28738 , where we nevertheless treated a double free in Regexp compilation as a vulnerability after a comprehensive assessment. We did the same for CVE-2024-27282 .

However, the Regexp documentation currently discusses untrusted patterns only in terms of denial of service, and recommends a timeout for them. It does not clearly say whether compiling an untrusted pattern is a use case that Ruby supports. We plan to discuss how to document this, and whether we treat this kind of issue as a vulnerability in Ruby, including whether to request CVE identifiers for these fixes. If we request any, we will update this page.

In the meantime, please refer to GitLab’s CVE identifiers listed above when you track these issues, for example in a security scanner.

Thanks to Johan Carlsson ( joaxcar ) for discovering the integer overflow fixed by #19020 through GitLab’s bug bounty program, and to GitLab for reporting these issues to us and coordinating the fixes.

items.title: LLMs are making formal software verification feasible at a much larger scale
items.content:
Keane Lucas, Aengus Lynch, Luna Tong, Luke Champine, Zygi Straznickas, Dino Distefano, Harshikaa Agrawal

Evyatar Ben Asher, Ava Howell, Sami Jawhar, Chris Rohlf, Nickolai Zeldovich

Nicholas Carlini, Rajashree Agrawal, Jason Gross

Most software is riddled with bugs, which AI can now easily find and exploit . The standard defenses against cyberattacks are no longer sufficient: we need ways to prove that code is free of bugs. Formal software verification could provide this guarantee, but it has historically required years of expert effort, making it impractical for most real-world projects. In a collaboration with Theorem , however, we show this is no longer the case: LLMs can now produce formal proofs at large scale, enabling new software development workflows that include proven security guarantees. Using Claude, we proved security properties at the assembly code level (RISC-V) in over 100 real-world open-source software libraries. To our knowledge, this represents the first large-scale effort to use AI to apply formal verification to production software at the assembly code level. While writing the proofs, Claude also discovered bugs that had eluded detection for years, despite trillions of test runs . As model capabilities continue to improve, we expect formal verification to become an essential part of secure software development.

Even mature, heavily tested software contains bugs, and LLMs are increasingly adept at finding them. The Linux kernel—one of the most well-tested pieces of software today, deployed on billions of devices worldwide—recently had over 1,000 vulnerabilities disclosed. With frontier models becoming more capable of chaining seemingly benign bugs into critical exploits, we need techniques that can detect and fix these bugs before they can be exploited in the wild.

Ideally, such techniques could find and patch all bugs, and then provide some proof that there are no more to be found. Formal verification is one way to do this. In formal verification, developers translate their code into a mathematical model, then try to prove that it always follows some defined set of security rules. If they fail to prove this, that means there could be a bug in the code that would violate a rule, and the nature of the failure implies what the bug might be. Repeating this process (after eliminating the cause of failure each time) will ultimately yield proof that the code is devoid of any bug that would violate those rules.

However, formal verification isn’t easy. Proofs can be many times larger than the original code, and writing them requires significant effort and a niche, highly specialized skill set. For instance, it took two person-years to implement the seL4 operating system kernel, but 20 person-years to formally verify it . Accordingly, formal verification has been practical only in truly mission-critical applications, such as Airbus’s avionics code .

But LLMs are making it far easier. Frontier models can now produce correctness proofs for real-world software fully autonomously. To demonstrate this, we asked Claude to prove useful security properties across 123 open-source libraries, including showing that some of their executable artifacts can never crash under certain conditions. Specifically, Claude proved that these programs will always exit normally without triggering memory-safety errors or failing assertions, for every input less than 64 MB and every modeled Linux operating system (OS) response and memory layout, under certain assumptions (namely that the program runs as a single-threaded static binary with a fixed memory budget on a RISC-V 1 CPU using Linux OS). This is still far away from fixing all possible bugs, but it does get us much closer than before and provides a roadmap toward that end.

We’re publishing a subset of these proofs so that anyone can verify and reuse them, along with the RISC-V and OS semantics . Theorem , our collaborator on this project, is also offering to run the same…

items.title: Expose only share links of a private service with caddy
items.content:
In my self-hosted infrastructure, most services are only reachable through my VPN. But some of them have a feature to share something with people outside: Immich has share links for albums and photos, Nextcloud has share links for files and folders.

My self-hosted infrastructure with Incus OS

I wanted to add some extra security, but the people receiving a link should not have to install a VPN client or create an account, they must be able to click on it and see the content.

The usual way to do this is to expose the whole service on the Internet, and then you have to trust the login page, the API and every route of the application. I found a simple pattern with the reverse proxy caddy that only lets in requests carrying a valid share link, and answers a 404 to everything else. The service itself is used to check if the link is valid.

In this blog post, you will learn how to use caddy to expose only the "share link" part of a service, how it works, and what it brings for security.

caddy has a directive named forward_auth . Before forwarding a request to the service, caddy sends a first request to another server (the "auth server"), and looks at the answer. If the answer is a success, the real request is forwarded, otherwise caddy returns the answer of the auth server to the client. This is usually used with software like Keycloak + oauth-proxy, to add a login page in front of an application.

caddy documentation: forward_auth directive

Here, the auth server is the service itself. Most applications have a route answering differently if a share key is valid or not, so we can ask the application "is this link valid?" before letting the request in.

The forward_auth directive is actually a shortcut for a reverse_proxy with a few options. I did not use forward_auth directly because I needed to rewrite the URL of the check request and to accept another status code than 2xx, so I wrote the long form with reverse_proxy and handle_response . This is also easier to understand, because everything is visible in the configuration.

caddy documentation: reverse_proxy, intercepting responses

the full service is reachable only through the VPN (or with an IP restriction), on a separate caddy instance (a single caddy server could work, but be sure to put IP restrictions on the internal vhost)

a public caddy site exposes only the routes needed by a guest, matched very strictly

for each request, caddy asks the service if the share key in the URL is valid

if it is valid, the request is forwarded, if not, caddy answers 404

every other URL gets the same 404, so a visitor cannot even know which software is behind

Immich is a photo and video library, I use it for my photos and videos. Browsing the library and uploading only works through the VPN, but I want to share albums with people who do not have direct access to it.

A share link in Immich looks like https://share.example.com/share/<key> , and then the web interface calls the API with ?key=<key> in the URL. I needed an API route that tells if a key is valid without doing anything. I found that requesting /api/users/me?key=<key> gives:

403 if the key is valid, because a share link is not allowed to read the user profile

So here, a 403 means the key is valid. The password of a share link (if there is one) does not matter for this check, Immich still asks for it after.

This is a side effect of how Immich checks permissions, not a feature made for this purpose, so a future version of Immich could change it. If this ever changes, the share links will answer 404 and I will notice quickly.

In the caddy configuration, I wrote a snippet (a reusable block of configuration, called with import ) taking the key as argument:

method GET and rewrite replace the method and the URL of the request sent to Immich, so whatever the visitor asked, Immich only receives GET /api/users/me?key=...

@valid_key status 403 matches the answer of Immich when the key is valid

items.title: Zero-day exploit completely defeats default Windows 11 BitLocker protections
items.content:
A zero-day exploit circulating online allows people with physical access to a Windows 11 system to bypass default BitLocker protections and gain complete access to an encrypted drive within seconds.

The exploit, named YellowKey, was published earlier this week by a researcher who goes by the alias Nightmare-Eclipse. It reliably bypasses default Windows 11 deployments of BitLocker, the full-volume encryption protection Microsoft provides to make disk contents off-limits to anyone without the decryption key, which is stored in a secured piece of hardware known as a trusted platform module (TPM). BitLocker is a mandatory protection for many organizations, including those that contract with governments.

When one disk volume manipulates another

The core of the YellowKey exploit is a custom-made FsTx folder. Online documentation of this folder is hard to find. As explained later, the directory associated with the file fstx.dll appears to involve what Microsoft calls the transactional NTFS , which allows developers to have “transactional atomicity” for file operations in transactions with a single file, multiple files, or ones that span multiple sources.

The steps for carrying out the bypass are simple:

Copy the custom FsTx folder from the Nightmare-Eclipse exploit page to an NTFS- or FAT-formatted USB drive

Connect the USB drive to the BitLocker-protected device

Boot up the device and immediately press and hold down the [Ctrl] key

There are at least two ways to accomplish the third step. One way is to boot into Windows, hold down the [Shift] key, click on the power icon, and click restart. Another is to power on the device and restart it as soon as Windows starts booting.

In either case, a command (CMD.EXE) prompt appears. The prompt has full access to the entire drive contents, allowing an attacker to copy, modify, or delete them. In a normal Windows Recovery flow, the attacker would need to enter a BitLocker recovery key. Somehow, the YellowKey exploit bypasses this safeguard. Multiple researchers, including Kevin Beaumont and Will Dormann , have confirmed the exploit works as described here.

It’s unclear what in the custom FsTx folder causes the bypass. Dormann said that it appears to be related to Transactional NTFS, which itself uses command-log file system under the hood. Dormann further noted that by looking at the Windows fstx.dll, one will see code that explicitly looks for \System Volume Information\FsTx in the FsTxFindSessions() function.”

The contents of this FsTx directory used in the YellowKey exploit reveal no strings related to RecoverySimulation.ini. It does, however, show the files and paths \??\C:\Windows\win.ini and

\??\X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini, “where X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini is what controls what WinRE [Windows Recovery] does when it fires up.”

Dormann, who is a senior principal vulnerability analyst at Tharros Labs, continued:

But what’s intriguing to me is: Why can the presence a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume affect the contents of ANOTHER VOLUME when it’s replayed? 🤔

In a normal WinRE session, you have a X:\Windows\System32 directory that has a winpeshl.ini file in it:

However, with the YellowKey exploit, it looks like Transactional NTFS bits on a USB Drive are able to delete the winpeshl.ini file on ANOTHER DRIVE (X:). And we get a cmd.exe prompt, with bitlocker unlocked instead of the expected Windows Recovery environment. While the TPM-only Bitlocker bypass is indeed interesting, I think the buried lede here is that a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume has the ability to modify the contents of another volume when it is replayed. To me, this in and of itself sounds like a vulnerability.

A Microsoft representative declined to answer questions sent by email about the reported vulnerability other than to say the company is investigating.

items.title: This AI aggregator leaked nearly 18 million files, including sex doll makers’ customer support chats
items.content:
302.ai exposed 17.6 million files after an Azure storage bucket was left publicly accessible, leaking 22.72TB of user data.

The 302.ai data leak included chat logs, generated images, videos, audio files, documents, and archived conversation files.

Exposed chat logs contained user prompts, assistant replies, timestamps, token costs, and sometimes personally identifiable information.

Researchers found enterprise data in the leak, including customer support chatbot logs linked to a prominent sex doll manufacturer.

Key Takeaways by nexos.ai , reviewed by Cybernews staff.

A security lapse at 302.ai, an AI aggregator, has exposed a massive amount of user information. The data leak affects both private and corporate users.

The AI aggregator leaked nearly 23TB of user data, or 17.6 million files, our researchers discovered. The information includes exactly what you’d expect: AI prompts, the machine’s replies, images, videos, and various corporate documents.

302.ai is a middleman between chatbot makers and end users. Its customers can access all major large language models (LLMs), such as ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, DeepSeek, Gemini, and many others.

After our research team reached out to the company, the exposed data was taken offline and is no longer publicly available. We have no evidence that malicious actors accessed or downloaded the data. However, if our team was able to find it, less impartial individuals may have, too.

items.content:
LibreOffice continues to enjoy strong demand following the release of version 26.8 in August. According to new figures from The Document Foundation , the open-source office suite recorded 9.4 million downloads over eight weeks, from August 24 to October 18, averaging more than one million downloads per week.

Even more impressive, LibreOffice’s total downloads for 2026 have already surpassed the entire 2025 figure, with ten weeks still remaining in the year.

The latest numbers follow the record-breaking first week of LibreOffice 26.8 , which saw 1,031,162 downloads shortly after release. Before the announcement, weekly downloads were slightly below one million but have remained above since.

And those 9.4 million downloads don’t tell the whole story. TDF explains that Windows updates are counted separately, as are downloads of older LibreOffice versions, which also continue to attract considerable interest.

To provide a broader picture, the foundation shared website traffic statistics for the same period. The main download website recorded 11.4 million visits, the Windows update website received about 90 million visits, and the site serving older LibreOffice releases registered nearly 39.7 million visits.

Of course, these figures represent website visits rather than actual downloads or installations, so they shouldn’t be added to the reported 9.4 million total.

As for what’s driving the growth, TDF acknowledges that it cannot provide a definitive answer. Since LibreOffice downloads are anonymous, the organization has no reliable way to determine exactly why more people are choosing the software.

“We like to think that the consistency of the LibreOffice project – which has been championing the concept of digital sovereignty and standard document formats for years – and the robustness of the software, which has never sought to be a clone of the most widely used office suite on the market but has always strived to forge its own path, are two very important factors that, in the long term, represent a significant advantage over all other products.”

Whatever the reasons, the numbers are impressive. This suggests interest in LibreOffice remains strong well after the initial excitement around version 26.8 . And with more than two months left in 2026, the project is on track to finish the year with substantially more downloads than in 2025.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

즐겨찾기 폴더 추가는 즐겨찾기 on 후 우측의 폴더 아이콘을 터치하여 추가할 수 있습니다.
